```ts
// stands beside a product's own entries is the product's decision rather than the user's: the user cannot
// place one, an entry placed before the decision stops being offered while the placement itself is KEPT
// (deciding the other way again restores it where they had put it), and saving, renaming, resetting and
// switching all still work with the workspace dialog as the way to them. Nothing is reported about their
// absence — it is a decision, not an omission. Workspaces the product DECLARED are untouched, and one that
// nothing offers is still reported.
// A rail or bar item naming a command nobody registered is dropped, like an orphaned menu entry.
interface ShellFeatures { content: ContentFeatures; sidebar: SidebarFeatures; rail: RailFeatures; workspaces: WorkspaceFeatures; windows: WindowFeatures; commands: CommandFeatures }
type ShellFeaturesInput = { [G in keyof ShellFeatures]?: Partial<ShellFeatures[G]> };
const DEFAULT_SHELL_FEATURES: ShellFeatures;           // the default workbench: every field true
const SHELL_FEATURES: InjectionToken<ShellFeatures>;
function provideShellFeatures(features: ShellFeaturesInput): EnvironmentProviders;
// The switches are LIVE. provideShellFeatures is the starting value; FeatureSwitches holds the current set:
class FeatureSwitches { current: Signal<ShellFeatures>; content: SwitchSignals<ContentFeatures>; sidebar; rail; workspaces; windows; commands; update(input: ShellFeaturesInput): void }
type SwitchSignals<G> = { [K in keyof G]: Signal<boolean> };   // switches.content.splitRight() — one read-only signal per switch
   // A switch removes the USER's routes (button, menu entry, drop target, shortcut) and never the capability: the distribution's
   // own code keeps reaching it through the services below. Switching off acts forward only (a split stays split). The shell
   // persists no switch; the next start begins from the declaration. Built-in commands/menu entries follow a switch live.
// The workbench from the distribution's own code — every action is the SAME code the control runs, with the same unsaved-work guards:
class PaneService { panes: Signal<readonly PaneFacts[]>; activePane: Signal<PaneHandle>; isSplit: Signal<boolean>; maximized: Signal<PaneHandle | null>; minimized: Signal<readonly PaneHandle[]>;
  splitRight(pane?: PaneHandle): void; splitDown(pane?: PaneHandle): void; closePane(pane?: PaneHandle): void; unsplit(): void;
  maximize(pane?: PaneHandle): void; minimize(pane?: PaneHandle): void; restore(pane?: PaneHandle): void; focus(pane: PaneHandle): void; moveTab(path: string, pane: PaneHandle): void; exists(pane: PaneHandle): boolean }
type PaneHandle;   // opaque, stable while the pane exists; a stale handle does nothing. Without a handle an action means the address pane.
interface PaneFacts { handle: PaneHandle; showing: string | null; itemCount: number; carriesAddress: boolean; maximized: boolean; minimized: boolean }
class WorkspaceService { workspaces: Signal<readonly Workspace[]>; activeId: Signal<string>; hasChanges: Signal<boolean>; changedIds: Signal<readonly string[]>;
  switchTo(id: string): Promise<void>; saveCurrent(name: string): Promise<void>; saveBaseline(): Promise<void>; rename(id: string, name: string): void;
  reset(id?: string): Promise<boolean>; resetAll(): Promise<boolean>; remove(id: string): Promise<boolean> }   // the three ask about unsaved work and answer whether they ran
class AppResetService { reset(options?: { workspaces?: boolean }): Promise<boolean> }   // asks once, also with the workspaces included
class SidebarService { regions: Signal<readonly SidebarFacts[]>; hiddenViews: Signal<readonly string[]>; isCollapsed(regionId: string): boolean; width(regionId: string): number;
  collapse(regionId: string): void; expand(regionId: string): void; toggle(regionId: string): void; setWidth(regionId: string, px: number): void; hideView(viewId: string): void; showView(viewId: string, regionId?: string): void }
interface SidebarFacts { regionId: string; collapsed: boolean; width: number }   // ids are the distribution's own (provideLayout regions, registered view ids)
class FontScaleService { scale: Signal<FontScale>; setScale(scale: FontScale): void }   // type FontScale = 'sm' | 'md' | 'lg' | 'xl'; 'md' imposes nothing
class PluginStoreService { open(): DialogRef; title: Signal<string> }   // opens the store dialog from your own control, with or without the built-in entries
type RetentionDefault = 'destroy' | 'retain';          // storage policy, set via provideShell({ retention })
   // retention: the app-wide default for HIDDEN surfaces — 'destroy' (default) destroys a hidden, clean
   // surface (tab switch, minimised pane, collapsed sidebar, closed compact drawer; VIEW_STATE is the survival path);
   // 'retain' keeps every hidden instance alive. A surface's own retain: 'always' | 'never' wins over this default.
function provideCommandPaletteEntry(options?: { bar?: string; slot?: BarSlot; order?: number }): EnvironmentProviders;  // LWF-05: a built badge-styled top-bar entry (search icon + OS-correct shortcut) opening shell.commandPalette. Opt-in; id 'shell.commandPaletteEntry' (omittable). Defaults: top-bar / end / order 5.
function provideQuickOpenEntry(options?: { bar?: string; slot?: BarSlot; order?: number }): EnvironmentProviders;  // the same badge for the other search: opens shell.quickOpen (mod+p) over open work. Opt-in and independent of the palette entry; id 'shell.quickOpenEntry' (omittable). Defaults: status-bar / start / order 5, apart from the palette badge on purpose. Either badge renders only while its command is registered and available — omit the command and the badge goes with it; with shortcuts off the badge stays and prints no chord.
// The palette itself (mod+k) matches by SUBSEQUENCE (fuzzy — "rst" finds "Reset list"), surfaces the commands the user
// last picked IN IT in a "Recently used" section on top (persisted at lw.shell.command-mru, most-recently-used behaviour —
// no other trigger adds to it: a command driven by its shortcut is one you can already reach without searching) and shows a
// keyboard-hint footer (↑↓ · ↵ · Esc). All host-internal — no authoring or distribution API.
// Quick-Open (amendment): a SECOND host command shell.quickOpen (mod+p) opens the same palette in tabs mode —
// every open tab across all content panes + every parameter-free, non-chromeless registered route, most-recent-first
// with relative time; Enter reveals the tab WHERE IT LIVES (a secondary pane is activated in place, not duplicated in the
// primary); → opens the tab's context menu. Source: ContentTabsService.quickOpenTargets / .revealContentTab
// (@loomweaver/shell, additive; QuickOpenTarget is exported). The tab last-active timestamps are session-only (no storage key).
function formatChord(chord: string): string;  // LWF-04: OS-correct chord for display — formatChord('mod+k') → '⌘K' (macOS) / 'Ctrl+K'. Same token vocabulary as Command.shortcut.
function provideShellRouter(extraRoutes?: Routes): (Provider | EnvironmentProviders)[];  // content-area routing; use INSTEAD of provideRouter([])
const Shell;   // the root component: <lw-shell></lw-shell>

interface ShellLayout { readonly regions: readonly LayoutRegion[]; }
interface LayoutRegion { readonly id: string; readonly type: 'bar'|'rail'|'panel'|'content'; readonly dock: 'top'|'bottom'|'left'|'right'|'center'; }

// from @loomweaver/plugin-sdk
function provideProductIdentity(identity: { name: string; tagline: string; logoUrl: string }): Provider;
```

## Canonical distribution

The shell is an ordinary standalone component, so it renders INSIDE the generated app rather than
replacing it. Angular's own shape is kept — `main.ts` bootstraps `App`, `App` renders `<lw-shell />`,
and every provider lives in `app.config.ts`. Identical under the Angular CLI and Nx.

```ts
// src/main.ts — unchanged from `ng new`
bootstrapApplication(App, appConfig).catch((err) => console.error(err));

// src/app/app.ts
@Component({ selector: 'app-root', imports: [Shell], templateUrl: './app.html' })
export class App {}

// src/app/app.html   →   <lw-shell />

// src/app/app.config.ts — the composition root
import { ApplicationConfig } from '@angular/core';
import { Shell, provideShell, provideShellRouter, provideLayout, providePlugins, provideTranslationNamespaces, provideCapabilityGrants } from '@loomweaver/shell';
import { provideProductIdentity } from '@loomweaver/plugin-sdk';
import { notesWeaver } from '@my/notes-weaver';

export const appConfig: ApplicationConfig = {
  providers: [
    provideShellRouter(),   // content-area routing — replaces provideRouter([])
    provideShell(),
    provideLayout({ regions: [
      { id: 'top-bar', type: 'bar', dock: 'top' },
      { id: 'activity', type: 'rail', dock: 'left' },
      { id: 'primary', type: 'panel', dock: 'left' },
      { id: 'main', type: 'content', dock: 'center' },
      { id: 'status-bar', type: 'bar', dock: 'bottom' },
    ] }),
    provideProductIdentity({ name: 'Notes Studio', tagline: 'product.tagline', logoUrl: 'logo.png' }),
    provideTranslationNamespaces('notes', 'product'),
    provideCapabilityGrants({ notes: ['contributions', 'ui', 'host'] }),
    // Optional: provideShellFeatures({ content, sidebar, rail, workspaces, windows, commands }) — switch user-facing gestures off
    // (every gesture is ON by default). Reordering: content.reorderTabs + rail.reorder + sidebar.reorderViews
    // let users sort within a band; sidebar.moveViews drags a VIEW between the left/right sidebars
    // (Alt+Shift+Left/Right by keyboard). A content tab's order lives on the pane that
    // holds it (in lw.shell.pane-trees), rail/view order in lw.shell.item-order — both user-local.
    // Uses @angular/cdk (a @loomweaver/shell peer dep).
    ...providePlugins(notesWeaver),   // variadic + returns an array: spread it
  ],
};
```

**Which provider does a decision go through?** There is deliberately no god-provider — folding these into one options bag would give each decision two doors. Indexed by intent: identity/layout/look = `provideProductIdentity` · `provideLayout` · the `--lw-*` tokens · `provideIcons` (replaces a shipped icon app-wide) · `provideTranslationOverrides` (rewords the shell) · `provideTranslationNamespaces` (adds your own strings). What users may DO = `provideShellFeatures` (gestures) · `provideShell({ omit })` (contributions) · `provideWorkspaces` (ready-made layouts); `shell.app.reset` ships, so "put the arrangement back" needs no wiring. What your own code may DO = the host services: `FeatureSwitches` (switches live and readable) · `PaneService` · `WorkspaceService` · `AppResetService` · `SidebarService` · `FontScaleService` · `PluginStoreService` — the same code the controls run, guards included, and a switched-off capability stays reachable to them. What ships inside = `providePlugins` + `provideCapabilityGrants` · `provideFramePlugins` · `providePluginCatalog` · `provideBarItems`/`provideRailItems`/`provideViews` · `provideCommandPaletteEntry`/`provideQuickOpenEntry`. What it talks to = `provideAuthSource` · `provideUnauthorizedRedirect` · `provideSettingsStore` · `provideWorkingStateStore` · `provideIdentityScopedStores` · `provideTabAddressResolver` · `provideShellRouter` · `provideShell({ serviceWorker, retention })`.

**Dev-mode composition report.** `loomweaver.report()` in the browser console (dev only, nothing reaches a production build) prints the declared regions, the switched-off capabilities and the omitted ids, then warns about what lands nowhere: an `omit` that **matched nothing**, naming the prefix you probably meant (bare `shell.permissions` hides a command or item of that id; the settings section of that name needs `setting:shell.permissions`, and the bare form fails silently), and a settings button or menu entry pointing at a **command no one registers** (or one your own `omit` removed) — the shell drops such a control rather than drawing a dead one, and this says why it vanished. One check does not wait for the console because it is decidable at startup and is warned about immediately: a bar/rail/view contribution aimed at a region the layout does not declare, or declares with another anatomy, naming the regions of the right type that do exist (the `status` versus `status-bar` mistake, which otherwise ships a silently empty status bar).

## Canonical weaver

```ts
import { Plugin } from '@loomweaver/plugin-sdk';
export const notesWeaver: Plugin = {
  manifest: { id: 'notes', name: 'Notes', capabilities: ['contributions', 'ui', 'host'] },
  activate(ctx) {
    ctx.registerCommand({ id: 'notes.add', title: 'notes.add', icon: 'add', shortcut: 'mod+enter', run: () => store.add() });
    ctx.registerSurface({ id: 'notes.list', docks: ['primary'], title: 'notes.list.title', icon: 'navigator',
      actions: [{ id: 'notes.list.add', icon: 'add', title: 'notes.add', command: 'notes.add' }], component: NotesListView });
    ctx.registerBarItem({ id: 'notes.add.btn', bar: 'status-bar', slot: 'start', icon: 'add', tooltip: 'notes.add', command: 'notes.add' });
    ctx.registerRailItem({ id: 'notes.settings', rail: 'activity', icon: 'settings', title: 'notes.settings', anchor: 'bottom', run: () => ctx.ui.openSettings() });
    ctx.registerSettingsSection({ id: 'notes', title: 'notes.name', group: 'settings.group.plugins', order: 100, rows: [] });
  },
};
```

## Setup essentials

- **Install:** `npm install @loomweaver/shell @loomweaver/plugin-sdk @angular/cdk @jsverse/transloco @ng-icons/heroicons @angular/service-worker@<your Angular version>`. Pin that last one to the `@angular/core` version already in the app: Angular packages peer-depend on each other by EXACT version, so the one Angular package an app does not already have is the one npm gets to choose, and it picks the newest — which demands a newer core and fails with `ERESOLVE`. Do **NOT** run `ng add @angular/pwa`: it writes `provideServiceWorker` into `app.config.ts`, which is exactly the registration `provideShell()` already owns (see `serviceWorker` above). The build also needs `"serviceWorker": "ngsw-config.json"` plus `"optimization": { "styles": { "inlineCritical": false } }` in its production configuration, and `.postcssrc.json` naming `@tailwindcss/postcss` beside `package.json` — **the scaffold writes all three**, so do not instruct anyone to add them by hand. State why they exist instead: without the PostCSS configuration the stylesheet is read as plain CSS and emits NO utility class, and without `inlineCritical: false` Angular's critical-CSS pass loads the stylesheet with an inline `onload` handler that the strict `script-src 'self'` blocks. Either one leaves the app completely unstyled while the build reports success.
- **Styles, two paths.** (a) **Tailwind 4** — `@import 'tailwindcss'; @source '../node_modules/@loomweaver/shell'; @import '@loomweaver/shell/styles/theme.css';`. Use semantic tokens only (`bg-surface`, `text-content`, `text-brand`); needed if you write Tailwind utilities of your own. (b) **Pre-compiled, Tailwind optional** — `@import '@loomweaver/shell/styles/shell.css';` alone (tokens + the `.lw-*` class contracts + every utility the shell's own templates use, ~67 KB / 11 KB gzipped). Take (b) when your product is themed with something else. Everything in it sits in cascade layers except two deliberate `html, body` rules, so your own unlayered CSS outranks ours — which means a foreign framework must be imported INTO a layer or its element rules (Bootstrap's Reboot: `button { border-radius: 0 }`) silently strip the chrome: `@import 'bootstrap/dist/css/bootstrap.css' layer(vendor);`. Re-theme by pointing the `--lw-*` tokens at your framework's variables in `@layer lw-tenant-theme` (`loom theme --name acme --preset bootstrap` writes that mapping for Bootstrap 5.3). Both halves are scaffolded: `loom distribution --name acme-studio --styles precompiled` emits (b) as the stylesheet, `--styles tailwind` (the default) emits (a).
- **Weaver body primitives:** semantic tokens · `prose-lw` · the host **`<lw-*>` custom elements** (used by tag, no `@loomweaver/shell` import; Angular weaver needs `schemas:[CUSTOM_ELEMENTS_SCHEMA]`): `<lw-icon name size>` · `<lw-button variant size>` (or the `.lw-btn` class contract on a native `<button>`) · `.lw-field` class contract on a native `<input>`/`<textarea>`/`<input type=date>` (+ `.lw-field--invalid`; no wrapper WC — native controls have full semantics) · `.lw-checkbox` / `.lw-switch` class contracts on a native `<input type=checkbox>` (switch adds `role=switch`) · `.lw-radio` / `.lw-range` class contracts on native `<input type=radio>` / `<input type=range>` (range needs an `aria-label`) · `.lw-progress` class contract on a native `<progress value max>` (bar) + `<lw-progress-ring value max size>` WC (ring — both need an `aria-label`; `size` is a CSS LENGTH like `2.5rem` [default], a bare number is silently ignored) · `.lw-badge` (+ `--brand`/`--success`/`--danger`) status pill on a `<span>` · `.lw-divider` on a native `<hr>` · `.lw-collapsible` on a native `<details>`/`<summary>` (+ `.lw-collapsible-body`; native disclosure, no JS) · `<lw-markdown source>` (marked+DOMPurify) · `<lw-select>`+`<lw-option>` (event `lw-select-change`) · `<lw-tooltip text position>` as last child of a `position:relative` trigger (a top-layer `[popover]` → NOT clipped inside a scrolling/virtualized or `transform`ed ancestor). **Custom elements do NOT survive `[innerHTML]`** — Angular's DomSanitizer strips them; use `<lw-*>` in your template, and for interactive bits on innerHTML content keep a preserved attribute (native `title`) or render a real element. Context menus, three cases: (1) host chrome — contribute items with `ctx.registerMenuItem` (host draws `<lw-menu>`) or a `menu?` slot on your rail/bar/view items; (2) your OWN in-process body — `ctx.ui.openMenu(items, {x,y})` (ad-hoc items with in-process `run`, host draws `<lw-menu>` at the cursor; body-level, never clipped); (3) your OWN sandboxed surface — draw `<lw-menu>` yourself and `openAt(x,y)` at the local cursor (in-process, no host RPC). **A weaver's OWN `customElements.define()` is the escape hatch (rung 4): allowed for trusted (build-time composed) plugins because they share the host document, but NOT a supported path — there is no `ctx` surface for it and it is the one contribution the platform cannot undo.** No `undefine` exists, so a tag outlives disable/update/uninstall; re-enabling a plugin runs `activate` again and an unguarded second `define()` throws `NotSupportedError`, which the runtime reports as an activation failure and the plugin loses ALL its contributions → always `if (!customElements.get(tag))`. It also does not survive a move to the sandbox rung (registry is per document; `<lw-*>` only reaches iframes because the host serves the script there), there is no collision handling (unlike first-wins `contributeIcons`) so prefix your own tags and never claim `lw-`, and a tag must not be offered to other plugins (undecided in-process, impossible across the sandbox). Prefer `<lw-*>`, the `.lw-*` class contracts and `ctx.ui`; if you do define one, paint it with the semantic tokens so theming reaches it.
- **i18n:** serve `@loomweaver/shell/i18n/**` at `/i18n/`; each namespace at `/i18n/<name>/{lang}.json` (nests under `<name>.*`, can't collide with host keys).
- **index.html:** `<lw-shell></lw-shell>`. **Angular 22 standalone, zoneless** (the shell declares zoneless change detection).

## Backend (optional, product-owned — the platform ships no server)

- The backend seam is expressed only as **frontend ports** with local/anonymous defaults: implement the `KeyValueStore` shape and provide it via `provideSettingsStore` (settings; the REST-worthy port) and optionally `provideWorkingStateStore` (working state; device-local by default), and feed `AuthSource` (a `Signal<AuthSnapshot>`) via `provideAuthSource`, against **your own backend** (any stack). The UI runs standalone with no backend.
- Settings persistence, auth/session, per-tenant secrets, credentialed egress and capability grants live in the product's backend — you need them anyway, and they can't be client-side. Third-party plugin credentialed egress will be a small **contract** (not a shipped server) defined when the first such plugin arrives.

## Letting an agent drive the product (`@loomweaver/ag-ui`)

The adapter that offers the workbench's OWN commands to an agentic backend speaking [AG-UI](https://docs.ag-ui.com) as tools. **Headless: no transport, no user interface, no agent** — you open the connection, you draw the conversation, you decide what the agent is. No Angular dependency and no observables: it is handed one event at a time, which is also why it is easy to test. `@ag-ui/core` and `@loomweaver/plugin-sdk` are PEER dependencies, so a weaver that also builds its own agent with `@ag-ui/client` resolves one copy of each. Do NOT hand-roll a dispatch over `ctx.invocableCommands()` / `ctx.invokeCommand()` — that is what this package already is.

```ts
import { commandTools } from '@loomweaver/ag-ui';
const tools = commandTools(ctx, {
  before: async (call) => DESTRUCTIVE.has(call.commandId)          // optional hook, may be async
    ? (await ctx.ui.confirm({ message: 'agent.confirm' })
        ? { decision: 'run' }
        : { decision: 'decline', reason: 'the user did not confirm it.' })
    : { decision: 'run' },
});
agent.runAgent({ tools: tools.list(), threadId, runId, messages, context: [] });  // ask again EVERY run
const answer = await tools.receive(event);   // for every event the run produces
if (answer) { messages.push(answer); }       // null when the event did not complete a call
```

- **`list()`** reads `ctx.invocableCommands()` at the moment you call it. **Never keep the answer**: what may be reached changes as plugins load and unload and as the session changes, and a stale list promises actions that are gone. Each entry is already narrowed by everything that would refuse the invocation — the command declared itself `callable`, the session meets its `access`, it belongs in this window, and your plugin holds `automation`.
- **`receive(event)`** answers a `ToolMessage` when an event completed a call and `null` otherwise; events that are not part of a tool call are ignored, so hand it everything without filtering. **`flush()`** closes a call an agent left open (`receive` already does it when the run reports finished or errored).
- **The `before` hook** answers `{ decision: 'run' }` (the default with no hook) · `{ decision: 'decline', reason }` (the workbench is never asked; the agent is told it did not run, and why) · `{ decision: 'answer', content }` (you serve the call yourself). **A decision can only NARROW**: letting a call through does not make it reachable, the workbench refuses what it always refused. `CommandToolOptions` carries only `before` today.
- **What crosses back**, all three faithfully, because the protocol has one `error` field and a tool that failed must be distinguishable from one that succeeded: *answered* → the value as `content` (a command declaring no answer reports plainly that it ran, rather than an empty string an agent would read as failure and retry) · *refused* → empty `content` + an `error` saying the command **did not run** · *failed* → empty `content` + an `error` saying it **ran and failed**.
- **The refusal wording is ONE wording** for every reason (no such command, not `callable`, session does not qualify, wrong window, no grant) — telling them apart would let an agent map what is installed by calling ids and reading the reason back.
- **Streamed and chunked calls.** A call arrives as a start, a stream of argument deltas and an end; calls in that form may interleave, because every event carries its own `toolCallId`. The convenience form, where one chunk event carries whichever fields it has, is inherently sequential: a chunk naming a new call closes the one before it. Arguments that are not readable JSON are refused before the workbench is asked; arguments that read fine but do not match what the command declared are refused by the workbench, which is where that check belongs.
- **The pieces, for less than the whole loop:** `toolFor(command)` / `toolsFor(commands)` (an `InvocableCommand` → a protocol `Tool`, declared arguments as JSON Schema) · `readArguments(json)` (streamed JSON → arguments the workbench can be handed, or `null`) · `resultFor(toolCallId, outcome)` (a `CommandOutcome` → the message that goes back, if you ran the call yourself) · `CommandAccess` (the slice of `ctx` this touches: `invocableCommands` + `invokeCommand`; narrow on purpose, because it states exactly what an agent reaches through here).
- Its stability follows the AG-UI protocol, not the platform. Full prose: docs/reference/agent-tools.md, worked example in docs/samples.md §10.

## Scaffolding & tooling (dev-time, deterministic)

Prefer generating over hand-wiring. Three dev-time `scope:tooling` packages, published on the same version line as the platform (none are part of the runtime `ctx` contract). One `ScaffoldDescriptor` per scaffold feeds all three adapters, so their options and output are identical; they differ only in what each is handed: the Nx adapter gets a virtual tree (writes AND changes existing files), the CLI gets a target directory (writes), MCP gets nothing (returns a file map).

- **`@loomweaver/devkit`** — the **Nx generator collection**, installed as a dev dependency (`npm i -D @loomweaver/devkit`; peers `@nx/devkit`). The fullest adapter: it is the only one that also *changes* files — it registers the project, adds the tsconfig alias, wires the weaver's i18n assets glob into the composing app and records a package the generated output needs in the consumer's manifest. Placement is read from the consumer workspace, not assumed: `--directory`, `--project-name`, `--import-path` (defaults to your root manifest's npm scope), `--app` (inferred when there is exactly one application, an error naming the candidates when there are several), `--tags`, `--prefix`, `--unit-test-runner`. Generators: `weaver` (feature-composable — flags `--command`/`--shortcut`/`--menu=<slot>`/`--bar-item`/`--settings`/`--about`/`--instanceable`/`--container`/`--agent`/`--access=<req>`/`--no-spec`; capabilities are derived from the chosen features, so it's correct-by-construction. `--instanceable` and `--container` shape the surface itself and are mutually exclusive: `--instanceable` **docks** it into `primary` and drops `routable`, because named instances exist only for a non-routable surface — the host does not carry `instanceable` onto a content route — and the rail item then uses `ctx.revealSurface`; `--container` makes it a routable container at `<id>/:id` holding a nested pane tree, emitting two children with `docks: []` whose components read the container's `:id` off an injected `ActivatedRoute`. `--agent` emits the AG-UI connection described above: a docked panel, `commandTools` with the `before` seam and one consequential command as an example, and a local stand-in in a single file that produces the protocol's own events — so the generated product demonstrates the whole path on the first serve, with no transport, credential or model generated for it. It implies `--command`, derives the `automation` capability, and states `@loomweaver/ag-ui` + `@ag-ui/core` as packages the output needs) · `frame-plugin` (framework-agnostic iframe/Penpal) · `distribution` (runnable composition root; `--styles precompiled` emits the Tailwind-free stylesheet, default `tailwind`) · `auth-source` · `settings-store` · `theme` (`--preset bootstrap` maps all 29 `--lw-*` tokens onto Bootstrap 5.3's `--bs-*`) · `layout`. E.g. `nx g @loomweaver/devkit:weaver --id=notes --settings --about`. Generated test wiring is `@nx/angular:unit-test` (Vitest). Plus the pure cores: `generate(recipe, input) → FileMap` and `validateManifest` / `validateI18nParity` / `validateCatalog` → `Finding[]`.
- **`@loomweaver/cli`** — the scaffolding **CLI** (adapter 2), the primary path for a product repo: no Nx workspace, no checkout, no assistant. `npx @loomweaver/cli weaver --id notes --command --shortcut 'mod+shift+n' --out src/lib/notes` · `list` · `validate-manifest` · `validate-i18n --dir <dir>` · `validate-catalog --file <path>`. Flags: `--out` (default `.`), `--dry-run` (also names files that already exist), `--force` (an existing file otherwise stops the run and is named), `--strict` (validation warnings fail the exit code, for CI). As the writing adapter it owns the guards: a path escaping `--out` is refused, a symlink inside `--out` is replaced rather than followed, and an unknown `--flag` fails the run instead of being dropped silently. Self-contained esbuild bundle, version == the platform version. It wraps the SAME pure core as MCP, so identical output; the difference is only who writes: the CLI does it, over MCP the assistant does.
- **`@loomweaver/mcp`** — an MCP server (stdio) exposing the same as tools for AI assistants: `list_generators` · `scaffold_*` · `validate_manifest` / `validate_i18n` / `validate_catalog` (return findings). **`scaffold_*` never touch the filesystem** — they return a file map of *relative* paths, and the client writes it, choosing the target root against its own layout (the server cannot know it). This is the mirror image of the Nx adapter: that one may write because it dictates the layout. Transport-neutral core; `nx bundle mcp` → self-contained `dist/main.mjs` (devkit + the MCP SDK inlined). Published as a bin package, so a product repo already consuming `@loomweaver/*` registers it in `.mcp.json` with `{ "command": "npx", "args": ["-y", "@loomweaver/mcp"] }` — scaffolding LoomWeaver artifacts without LoomWeaver's Nx workspace. Remote/HTTP transport is a thin later layer over the same `createMcpServer()`. (See `platform/libs/tooling/mcp/README.md`.)

- A PLUGIN's public API is exactly `@loomweaver/plugin-sdk`'s exports (typings ship in the package); nothing else is public API for a plugin.
-   A DISTRIBUTION additionally composes `@loomweaver/shell`'s exports (provideShell, provideShellRouter, the provide* ports, StateSyncService, PopoutService, PluginInstallService, …) — everything in its packed .d.ts.
